entry.name: Question
entry.pattern: Host:SyntacticExpression => Meaning:Question[set of logically possible answers]

dimensions.form: No unique syntactic form: the semantic category applies to headed Clauses of more than one type, coordinations, and constructionally licensed non-clausal expressions
dimensions.meaning: A structured set of logically possible answers, closed or open according to the variables and alternatives presented
dimensions.function: Makes resolution of an informationally incomplete answer space relevant; inquiry is the prototype but not a condition of membership
dimensions.distribution: A semantic layer over syntactic hosts, including interrogative and declarative Clauses, multi-Clause coordinations, and reduced or non-headed question expressions

1.definition: A semantic category in which an expression defines a set of logically possible answers
1.details: Question is not a clause type and is not identified with the pragmatic act of making an inquiry. A question determines answerhood conditions: a closed question presents a delimited answer set, while an open question contains a variable whose possible values differentiate the answers. An answer supplies the relevant missing information; a conversational response need not do so. Questions can serve acknowledgement, wondering, examination, exposition, and indirect speech acts as well as information-seeking inquiry, and the same semantic category can be realized by syntactically different hosts (CGEL Ch. 10 §§4.1–4.3, pp. 865–72).

examples.note: Closed-interrogative Clause defining positive and negative answers
Open-interrogative Clause defining answers by values of the variable who
Declarative Clause carrying question meaning without becoming interrogative
Reduced syntactic host with question meaning; it is not thereby a Clause

constraints.description: Membership is determined by the answer set an expression defines, not by interrogative morphology, word order, punctuation, or any single clause type.
An answer must resolve the relevant alternative or assign a value to the relevant variable; other conversational responses can be appropriate without constituting answers.
Information-seeking inquiry is a prototypical use rather than the definition: acknowledgement, wondering, quiz, expository, rhetorical, and indirect-act uses remain possible.
When the host is a Clause, it independently satisfies (Subject +) Head:VP. A coordination or constructionally licensed fragment may host question meaning without being reclassified as a Clause.
Independent dimensions distinguish polar, alternative, and variable questions; information and direction questions; neutral and biased questions; and ordinary and echo questions.

projection.target: Recognizing Question meaning predicts a structured class of congruent answers, a principled distinction between answers and merely appropriate responses, informational incompleteness resolvable by an answer, and semantic contrasts of answer-space, bias, direction, and echo status that remain independent of the host's clause type
projection.evidence: Closed, open, declarative, coordinated, and reduced realizations differ formally but preserve answer-set organization; the same organization persists across inquiry, acknowledgement, wondering, examination, exposition, and indirect-act uses

grounds.note: Defines questions by answer sets, distinguishes answers from responses, and cross-classifies questions independently of clause type
The answer-set generalizations recur across closed, open, declarative, coordinated, and reduced hosts

known_boundary_items: Interrogative is a syntactic property of particular words, phrases, and Clauses; it is neither necessary nor by itself a definition of Question meaning.
Question punctuation is an orthographic cue and does not determine semantic membership by itself.
A reduced or non-headed question expression may have Question meaning without satisfying the VP-headed definition of Clause.

relatedConstructions.notes: Many questions have a Clause host, which remains independently defined as (Subject +) Head:VP
Closed interrogatives are the characteristic syntactic host of closed questions, but clause type and Question meaning are distinct
Open interrogatives characteristically host variable questions without defining the semantic category
Declarative Clauses can host Question meaning while retaining declarative clause type
A coordination of Clauses may jointly present one alternative question while remaining a non-headed coordination
Constructionally licensed non-headed expressions may carry Question meaning without becoming Clauses

grounds.note: Treats question at the semantic level as an answer-set category and distinguishes it from both clause type and pragmatic inquiry
Question is a semantic category applied to syntactic hosts; clausal hosts retain the strict (Subject +) Head:VP ontology

curious.title: What makes something a question
curious.summary: A question is defined by the set of possible answers it opens, not by its word order or question mark.
curious.body:
Have you seen it? leaves two possible answers, yes or no. Who broke it? leaves open who did it. Which one? is a short phrase that does the same job, and You're leaving? shows that a statement can also act as a question.

So what makes something a question is the set of answers it defines, not one particular grammar. This dictionary says a question isn't the same as an act of inquiry either: questions can also acknowledge, wonder, examine or explain. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Find a sentence that doesn't look like a question but would still get an answer if you said it to someone. What answer would it get?

teacher.summary: Frames question as a meaning category (a set of possible answers) that different sentence types can carry.
teacher.explain: Question is a semantic category: an expression defines a set of logically possible answers. It is not a clause type and is not the same as the act of inquiry. A closed question presents a delimited answer set (Have you seen it?), an open question contains a variable (Who broke it?), a declarative clause can carry question meaning (You're leaving?) and a reduced expression can too (Which one?, which isn't thereby a Clause). An answer supplies the missing information; a conversational response needn't. This dictionary says punctuation and word order don't fix membership, and it marks the account provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary separates the clause types (closed and open interrogative) from the semantic category Question.
watch_for: A learner might think a question must start with an auxiliary or a question word.
A learner might think a question mark makes something a question.
A learner might treat any reply as an answer, when an answer resolves the open alternatives.
teacher.activity: Give students four cards, each carrying a different question form. They list the possible answers each defines and sort replies into answers and merely appropriate responses.

child.hook: How do you know something is a question?
child.explain: A question comes with a set of possible answers. Have you seen it? can be answered with yes or no. Who broke it? can be answered by saying who.
child.play: Ask a friend a question that needs a yes or no. Then ask one that starts with who. Which kind was easier to answer?

checked.note: Fixed: child explain no longer defines a question as asking for an answer or says Who broke it? needs a name (this dictionary lists rhetorical and other uses, and an answer need only identify who); curious body says Who broke it? leaves open who did it; teacher terms drops the yes/no and wh-question equations, which this dictionary keeps apart from the clause types. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' wording.
